# Lynn Conway
Lynn Conway (1938–2024) was a pioneering computer scientist and electrical engineer, notable for her groundbreaking work in computer architecture, very-large-scale integration (VLSI) design methodology, and transgender rights activism. Born in Mount Vernon, New York, she initially studied at MIT before interruptions due to gender dysphoria and later transitioned. After earning degrees from Columbia University, she joined IBM Research in 1964, contributing to the Advanced Computing Systems project and innovating multiple-issue out-of-order dynamic instruction scheduling—the first superscalar architecture. Fired by IBM in 1968 after revealing her intent to transition, she restarted her career stealthily in roles at Computer Applications, Inc., Memorex, and Xerox PARC.
At Xerox PARC, Conway led the "LSI Systems" group, co-founding the revolutionary Mead–Conway VLSI design methodology with Carver Mead. Their 1980 textbook became foundational in chip design education globally, spurring advances in electronic design automation, integrated circuit prototyping, and semiconductor manufacturing infrastructure, exemplified by the MOSIS prototyping service. Conway also taught at MIT and contributed to DARPA's Strategic Computing Initiative before becoming a professor and associate dean at the University of Michigan. Her influence significantly shaped modern VLSI design, fostering a wave of tech startups.
In later years, Conway publicly shared her gender transition story, becoming an outspoken transgender rights advocate. She fought for awareness, medical resources, and employment protections, opposing pathologization of transgender identities and academic misconduct in related research. She received numerous honors, including IEEE Fellow, the Computer Pioneer Award, National Academy of Engineering membership, and lifetime achievement awards. In 2020, IBM publicly apologized for firing her and presented her with a Lifetime Achievement Award. Conway died in 2024 at age 86, leaving a lasting legacy in computing and social justice.
